lesson.title: Stress, strain and stiffness

lead.text: The last lesson ended with a force in each bar of a truss. A force on its own does not say whether a bar will cope. A pull of 24 kN is nothing to a thick steel bar, and it may be more than a thin steel rod can take.

Suppose a rod hangs a 24 kN load and you are unsure it is strong enough. One fix is to hang the load from three identical rods side by side. They share the load equally, so each carries 8 kN, a third of the original. Another fix is to use a single rod three times as fat. Either way, the load has three times as much steel to work with.

What the steel feels depends on the force and on how much material shares it. A rod's cross-section is the shape you would see if you sliced it at right angles to its length, and its area is measured in square millimetres (mm²). Three rods side by side have three times the cross-sectional area of one. The next screen puts force and area into one number.

diagram.alt: A 24 kN load hung from a ceiling by steel rods, with a circle beside the rods for each rod's cross-section drawn to scale. One rod carries all 24 kN. Three rods carry 8 kN each and have three times the area in all. One thick rod has a larger circle.
diagram.caption: More steel in the cross-section means less force on each square millimetre. The circles show each rod's cross-section at the same scale. Use the buttons to compare the three arrangements.

lead.text: Think about the three rods on the last screen. Two rods share a load in just the same way.

Engineers combine force and area into one number called stress: the force carried by each square millimetre of the cross-section. In symbols σ = F ÷ A, where σ (sigma) is the stress, F is the force and A is the cross-sectional area. Take a rod of 200 mm² that holds the 24 kN load alone. That is 24,000 N ÷ 200 mm² = 120 N/mm².

One newton per square millimetre is called a megapascal (MPa), so that rod is at 120 MPa. Using newtons and square millimetres gives megapascals directly, which is why kilonewtons must be converted to newtons first. Hang the same load from three such rods and each carries 8,000 N on 200 mm², which is only 40 MPa. The picture compares a thin rod with a thick one.

afterFigure.text: Stress decides whether steel gives way, and force alone does not. A rod that is comfortable at 40 MPa may be in trouble at 400 MPa, whatever force produced it. The same force on twice the area gives half the stress, which is why a thick bar is safer than a thin one.

lead.text: Convert the load to newtons first, then divide by the area in mm².

Stress describes what the steel is asked to carry. Next comes what the rod does in response. It stretches. A pulled rod gets a little longer, and how much longer depends on how long it was to begin with. A 4 m rod stretches twice as much as a 2 m rod of the same steel under the same stress. So stretch is best measured as a fraction of the original length.

That fraction is called strain, written ε (epsilon). It is the extension δ (delta), the amount the rod lengthens, divided by the original length L: ε = δ ÷ L. Take a rod 5 m long, which is 5,000 mm, that stretches by 4 mm. Its strain is 4 ÷ 5,000 = 0.0008. Strain is a ratio of two lengths, so it has no unit, and both lengths must be in the same unit before you divide.

diagram.alt: A steel bar fixed at one end and pulled at the other. First the whole 5,000 mm bar is shown with its original length marked and a note that the 4 mm extension is too small to see. Second the end of the bar is enlarged so the 4 mm extension is visible, with the strain worked out.
diagram.caption: Strain is the extension as a fraction of the original length. Use the buttons to see the whole rod and then the extension enlarged.

Strain ε = δ ÷ L = 4 ÷ 5,000 = 0.0008.</text></svg>

lead.text: Both lengths must be in the same unit before you divide.

Stress and strain are linked. While the stress stays low enough for the rod to spring back when released, the strain is proportional to the stress. Double the stress and the strain doubles. The ratio between them belongs to the material and is called Young's modulus, written E. So stress = E × strain, or strain = stress ÷ E.

E measures stiffness: how much stress it takes to produce a given stretch. Structural steel has an E of about 200 GPa. Aluminium alloys have about 70 GPa, so under the same stress an aluminium bar stretches nearly three times as much as a steel bar of the same length. The picture shows the two side by side.

afterFigure.text: Put E in the same unit as the stress before dividing. 1 GPa is 1,000 MPa, so steel is 200,000 MPa. A steel bar at 80 MPa has a strain of 80 ÷ 200,000 = 0.0004. E says how much a bar stretches. How much stress it can survive is a separate property, covered at the end of the lesson.

steps.headline: A 3,000 mm steel bar (E = 200 GPa) carries a stress of 60 MPa. How far does it stretch?

lead.text: Here is the whole method, from the stress to the stretch.

workedSteps.text: Write E in MPa so that it matches the unit of stress.
Strain is stress divided by E.
Stretch is strain times the original length.

steps.headline: The bar is 2,000 mm long and its steel has E = 200 GPa. At 50 MPa, how far does it stretch?

lead.text: The method is the same as in the worked example.

workedSteps.text: Strain is stress divided by E.
Multiply the strain by the original length, in mm.

lead.text: Same method, different material. Aluminium is less stiff than steel.

So far every bar has sprung back to its original length when the load was removed. That holds only up to a limit. Plot stress against strain for a steel bar and the line is straight at first, at a slope of E. Where the straight part ends is the yield stress. Beyond it the bar stretches a lot for a small rise in stress, and when the load is taken off it does not return all the way. It keeps a permanent stretch, called permanent set.

Keep pulling and the stress rises further, up to the ultimate strength, the highest stress the bar can hold. After that the bar thins at one spot and breaks. A stronger steel might have a yield stress of 355 MPa and an ultimate strength of 510 MPa. The picture loads such a bar to two levels, one below its yield stress and one above it.

afterFigure.text: Designers keep working stress well below the yield stress, so that the structure springs back every time the load is removed. The next lesson asks how far below.

lead.text: Compare the load with both strengths before you decide.

lesson.orientation: Relate force per area to stretch per length through Young's modulus.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Stretch a rubber band and you can see it get longer. A steel rod does the same, by an amount too small for the eye to notice. A 2 m steel tie pulled hard may lengthen by only a millimetre or so. A designer still needs to know how much, and whether the tie will return to its old length when the load is removed.

The last lesson gave the force in each bar of a truss. A force of 40 kN is nothing to a thick steel bar and is ruinous to a thin wire. The force alone does not say whether a bar is safe, and it does not say how far the bar will stretch either. Something else has to be measured first.
This lesson follows one steel rod as the load on it grows. We first work out how hard the steel is working, then how far it stretches, and finish at the load where it stops springing back.

intro.promise: By the end you'll turn a load into a stress, and a stress into a stretch.

recap.keyIdea: Stress is force over area, and in the elastic range it is E times the strain. Past yield, a bar keeps a permanent stretch.

blocks.text: Back at the hanging rod, you turned a 20 kN pull on 400 mm² into 50 MPa, and found that it stretches a 2,000 mm steel bar by 0.5 mm. The same stress stretches a 1,400 mm aluminium bar by 1 mm, because aluminium is less stiff.

recap.nextHook: A real design never runs a bar at its limit, and the next lesson works out how much margin to leave below the yield stress.

questions.prompt: A 20 kN load hangs from a single steel rod. You replace the rod with two identical rods side by side, sharing the load equally. What force, in kN, does each rod carry?
hints: The two rods share the load equally.
Together they carry the whole 20 kN.
Divide the load between the two rods.
questions.onCorrect: 10 kN each. Each rod now carries half the force, but it is the force per area that matters.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole load on one rod. The two rods share it.
Two rods do not double the load. Together they carry exactly the load.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two identical rods share the 20 kN equally, so each carries 20 ÷ 2 = 10 kN.

questions.prompt: A bar carries a fixed force. Its cross-sectional area is doubled. What happens to the stress?
hints: Stress is force divided by area.
questions.onCorrect: Stress is F/A, so doubling the area halves the stress for the same force.

misconceptions.feedback: Stress is force divided by area, so more area means less stress.
The force is the same, but it is spread over a larger area.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It halves. σ = F/A, so doubling A halves σ.

questions.prompt: A steel bar with a cross-section of 400 mm² carries a 20 kN axial pull. Find the stress in MPa.
hints: Convert the load to newtons.
Divide by the area in mm²; 1 N/mm² is 1 MPa.
Calculate 20,000 ÷ 400.
questions.onCorrect: 50 MPa: force in newtons over area in square millimetres gives megapascals directly.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves the load in kN, so it is a thousand times too small. Convert to newtons first.
That is the force in newtons. Divide it by the area.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 2 without converting. The lengths must be in the same unit.

Use the length in mm.

questions.prompt: An aluminium bar (E = 70 GPa) 1,400 mm long carries a stress of 50 MPa. Find its stretch in mm.
hints: Write E in MPa: 70 GPa is 70,000 MPa.

questions.prompt: A steel bar with yield stress 250 MPa and ultimate strength 400 MPa is loaded to 300 MPa, then unloaded. What happens?
hints: Compare 300 MPa with both strengths.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It keeps a permanent stretch. 300 MPa is past yield but below the ultimate strength, so the bar survives with a permanent set.

questions.onCorrect: 300 MPa is past yield but below the ultimate strength, so the bar survives with a permanent set.

misconceptions.feedback: A bar only springs back fully below its yield stress. This load is above it.
